subject: Business Models
title: Razor and Blade
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Razor and Blade.

hook.text: King Gillette gave away razors in 1904 and made a fortune on replacement blades. The model persists everywhere.

buildup.text: Sell the base product cheap (or free). Lock customers in. Profit from ongoing consumable purchases.

discovery.text: Printers, Keurig, game consoles, and electric toothbrushes all use razor-blade economics.

twist.text: Dollar Shave Club reversed it: cheap blades, direct to consumer. It sold to Unilever for $1 billion.

climax.text: Razor-blade is powerful but vulnerable. Cheap alternatives can break the consumable lock-in.

punchline.text: Free razor, expensive blades since 1904. 120 years later, the model still works.

quiz.question: How did Dollar Shave Club disrupt the razor-blade model?
options: Cheaper blades sold directly to consumers

details.summary: The razor-and-blade model sells a base product at low or zero margin to lock customers into purchasing high-margin consumables. Gillette popularized this approach, and it now appears in printers and ink, game consoles and titles, and coffee machines and pods.
details.whyItMatters: This model creates recurring revenue from an installed base of locked-in customers. Understanding it reveals why companies sell hardware cheaply and shows how consumable lock-in drives some of the most profitable businesses.
takeaways: A low-margin base product drives demand for high-margin consumables
Customer switching costs create long-term recurring revenue streams
Printers, game consoles, and coffee machines all use this pattern

faq.question: How does the razor-and-blade model create customer lock-in?
faq.answer: The base product is designed to work only with proprietary consumables. Switching requires buying a new base product, which customers resist after their initial investment. This creates high switching costs that sustain consumable purchases over years.

faq.question: What is the reverse razor-and-blade model?
faq.answer: Companies sell a premium base product at high margins and offer cheap or free consumables. Apple sells expensive iPhones but offers the App Store ecosystem. This approach attracts customers with low ongoing costs after the initial premium purchase.
